personas/marvin-minsky/resumen.texto: American computer scientist, co-founder of the MIT artificial intelligence laboratory. He signed the Dartmouth proposal (1955) and wrote “Perceptrons” (1969) with Seymour Papert; 1969 Turing Award.

personas/rosenblatt/resumen.texto: American psychologist. At the Cornell Aeronautical Laboratory he created the perceptron (1958), an artificial neural network that learned to classify images.

personas/licklider/resumen.texto: American psychologist and computer scientist. In “Man-Computer Symbiosis” (1960) he envisioned interactive computing, and as the first director of ARPA's computing office (1962-1964) he funded the research that led to ARPANET.

personas/engelbart/resumen.texto: American engineer at the Stanford Research Institute. He invented the mouse and in 1968 publicly demonstrated a system with hypertext, windows, shared editing and videoconferencing. 1997 Turing Award.

personas/alan-kay/resumen.texto: American computer scientist. At Xerox PARC he envisioned the Dynabook, a portable personal computer, and led the development of Smalltalk and windowed interfaces; 2003 Turing Award.

personas/ken-thompson/resumen.texto: American computer scientist. In 1969 at Bell Laboratories he wrote the first version of Unix and later the B language; 1983 Turing Award with Dennis Ritchie. He later took part in the design of UTF-8 and the Go language.

personas/dennis-ritchie/resumen.texto: American computer scientist at Bell Labs. He created the C programming language and developed Unix with Ken Thompson; Turing Award in 1983.

personas/kernighan/resumen.texto: Canadian computer scientist at Bell Labs. He wrote “The C Programming Language” (1978) with Dennis Ritchie and co-created the AWK language.

personas/metcalfe/resumen.texto: American engineer. At Xerox PARC he invented Ethernet (1973) with David Boggs and later founded the company 3Com; Turing Award in 2022.

personas/hopfield/resumen.texto: American physicist. In 1982 he described a neural network that stores and retrieves memories as minimum-energy states; he shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics with Geoffrey Hinton.

personas/rumelhart/resumen.texto: American cognitive psychologist at the University of California, San Diego. With Hinton and Ronald Williams he published in 1986 the paper that popularized backpropagation for training neural networks.

personas/hinton/resumen.texto: British-Canadian computer scientist. He popularized backpropagation (1986) and with his students won ImageNet in 2012 with AlexNet; Turing Award in 2018 and Nobel Prize in Physics in 2024 with John Hopfield. In 2023 he left Google to warn about the risks of AI.

personas/sergey-brin/resumen.texto: Computer scientist born in Moscow and raised in the US. With Larry Page he developed at Stanford the search engine they founded as Google in 1998.

personas/larry-page/resumen.texto: American computer scientist. He devised the PageRank algorithm and founded Google with Sergey Brin in 1998; he was CEO of Google and later of Alphabet until 2019.

personas/krizhevsky/resumen.texto: Computer scientist, a student of Geoffrey Hinton in Toronto. He designed AlexNet, the convolutional neural network trained on graphics processors that won the 2012 ImageNet competition.

personas/hassabis/resumen.texto: British researcher, co-founder of DeepMind (2010), acquired by Google in 2014. He led AlphaGo and AlphaFold and shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with John Jumper and David Baker.

personas/john-jumper/resumen.texto: American theoretical chemist at DeepMind. He led the development of AlphaFold 2, which predicts the structure of proteins; Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2024.

personas/vaswani/resumen.texto: Computer scientist, first author of “Attention Is All You Need” (2017), the Google paper that introduced the transformer architecture.

personas/paul-baran/resumen.texto: American engineer at the RAND Corporation. Between 1960 and 1964 he proposed a distributed network that would split messages into blocks to survive a nuclear attack, one of the origins of packet switching.

personas/donald-davies/resumen.texto: British computer scientist at the National Physical Laboratory. In 1965–1966, unaware of Baran's work, he proposed packet switching, a term he coined, and built the laboratory's network.

personas/steve-crocker/resumen.texto: American computer scientist. As a student at UCLA he wrote RFC 1 (1969) and created the “Request for Comments” document series used to define internet protocols.

personas/vint-cerf/resumen.texto: American computer scientist. With Bob Kahn he designed the TCP/IP protocol, the basis of the internet, in 1974; Turing Award in 2004.

personas/bob-kahn/resumen.texto: American engineer at the ARPA agency. With Vint Cerf he designed TCP/IP to interconnect different networks; Turing Award in 2004.

personas/mockapetris/resumen.texto: American computer scientist at the University of Southern California's Information Sciences Institute. In 1983 he designed the Domain Name System (DNS).

personas/berners-lee/resumen.texto: British computer scientist. At CERN he proposed the World Wide Web in 1989 and wrote the first server and the first browser; since 1994 he has directed the World Wide Web Consortium (W3C). Turing Award in 2016.

personas/andreessen/resumen.texto: American programmer and investor. As a student at the University of Illinois's NCSA he wrote the Mosaic browser (1993) with Eric Bina; he later co-founded Netscape.

personas/darwin/resumen.texto: English naturalist. After the voyage of the Beagle (1831–1836) he developed the theory of evolution by natural selection, published in “On the Origin of Species” (1859).

personas/mendel/resumen.texto: Augustinian monk from Brno. Through crosses of pea plants he formulated the laws of inheritance (1866), which were ignored until their rediscovery in 1900.

personas/fleming/resumen.texto: Scottish bacteriologist at St Mary's Hospital in London. In 1928 he observed that a mold, Penicillium, inhibited the growth of bacteria: penicillin. He shared the 1945 Nobel Prize in Medicine with Florey and Chain.

personas/florey/resumen.texto: Australian pathologist at Oxford. With Ernst Chain and his team he purified penicillin and tested it on animals (1940) and on patients (1941); he shared the 1945 Nobel Prize in Medicine with Fleming and Chain.

personas/banting/resumen.texto: Canadian physician. At the University of Toronto in 1921, with Charles Best, he isolated insulin, used from 1922 to treat diabetes; he shared the 1923 Nobel Prize in Medicine with John Macleod.

personas/salk/resumen.texto: American virologist at the University of Pittsburgh. He developed the first effective polio vaccine, using inactivated virus, approved in 1955; he did not patent it.

personas/watson/resumen.texto: American biologist. In 1953, at the Cavendish Laboratory, he proposed the double helix of DNA with Francis Crick (Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1962); he later directed Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory and, between 1988 and 1992, the Human Genome Project. His statements on race and intelligence cost him his honorary positions.

personas/crick/resumen.texto: British physicist and biologist. With Watson he proposed the structure of DNA (1953), formulated the central dogma of molecular biology (1958) and worked on deciphering the genetic code; Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1962. From 1976 he studied consciousness at the Salk Institute.

personas/rosalind-franklin/resumen.texto: British chemist, an expert in X-ray diffraction. At King's College London she obtained, with Raymond Gosling, “Photo 51” of DNA, which Watson and Crick saw without her knowledge. She died at 37, before the 1962 Nobel Prize, which is not awarded posthumously.

personas/nirenberg/resumen.texto: American biochemist at the National Institutes of Health. In 1961, with Heinrich Matthaei, he deciphered the first “codon” of the genetic code; Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1968.

personas/mullis/resumen.texto: American biochemist at the company Cetus. In 1983 he devised the polymerase chain reaction (PCR), which copies a DNA fragment millions of times; Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1993. He later denied that HIV causes AIDS.

personas/ian-wilmut/resumen.texto: British embryologist at the Roslin Institute. He led the team that cloned Dolly the sheep (1996), the first mammal cloned from an adult cell.

personas/venter/resumen.texto: American biologist. With the company Celera he sequenced the human genome in competition with the public project and published his version in 2001; in 2010 his institute created a bacterium with a synthetic genome.

personas/doudna/resumen.texto: American biochemist at the University of California, Berkeley. With Emmanuelle Charpentier she showed in 2012 that the CRISPR-Cas9 system can be programmed to cut DNA; Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2020.

personas/charpentier/resumen.texto: French microbiologist. While researching the immune system of bacteria in Umeå (Sweden), she described the CRISPR-Cas9 tool with Doudna (2012); Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2020. She heads a unit of the Max Planck Society in Berlin.

personas/kariko/resumen.texto: Hungarian-American biochemist. At the University of Pennsylvania she showed with Drew Weissman (2005) that modifying nucleosides prevents messenger RNA from causing inflammation, the basis of mRNA vaccines; Nobel Prize in Medicine in 2023.

personas/weissman/resumen.texto: American immunologist at the University of Pennsylvania. With Katalin Karikó he developed the modified messenger RNA used in COVID-19 vaccines; Nobel Prize in Medicine in 2023.

personas/montagnier/resumen.texto: French virologist at the Pasteur Institute. His laboratory isolated in 1983 the virus later named HIV; he shared the 2008 Nobel Prize in Medicine with Françoise Barré-Sinoussi. In his final years he upheld theories rejected by the scientific community.

personas/barre-sinoussi/resumen.texto: French virologist at the Pasteur Institute, first author of the 1983 paper that described the retrovirus later named HIV; Nobel Prize in Medicine in 2008.

personas/tsiolkovski/resumen.texto: Russian schoolteacher and theorist from Kaluga. In 1903 he published the rocket equation and argued that liquid-fuel rockets would make space travel possible.

personas/goddard/resumen.texto: American physicist at Clark University. In 1919 he published his theory for reaching high altitudes with rockets, and on March 16, 1926 he launched the first liquid-fuel rocket.

personas/von-braun/resumen.texto: German engineer. At Peenemünde he led the development of the V-2 missile, produced with forced labor by concentration camp prisoners; brought to the United States in 1945, he led the Saturn V rocket of the Apollo program.

personas/korolev/resumen.texto: Soviet engineer, chief designer of the space program. He was imprisoned in the Gulag (1938–1944); he led the R-7 missile, Sputnik and Gagarin's flight, and his identity was kept secret until his death.

personas/gagarin/resumen.texto: Soviet pilot. On April 12, 1961 he became the first human to travel into space, in one orbit around the Earth aboard Vostok 1; he died in a plane crash in 1968.

personas/neil-armstrong/resumen.texto: American astronaut. Commander of Apollo 11, on July 20, 1969 he became the first human to set foot on the Moon.

personas/keeling/resumen.texto: American chemist at the Scripps Institution of Oceanography. From 1958 he precisely measured atmospheric carbon dioxide at Mauna Loa and showed its year-on-year increase: the Keeling curve.

personas/manabe/resumen.texto: Japanese-American meteorologist at the Geophysical Fluid Dynamics Laboratory (NOAA). Using numerical models, he calculated in 1967 how much doubling CO₂ would warm the Earth; Nobel Prize in Physics in 2021.

personas/maxwell/resumen.texto: Scottish physicist. He unified electricity, magnetism and light in a field theory (1865) and was the first director of the Cavendish Laboratory in Cambridge.

personas/edison/resumen.texto: American inventor and businessman. In his Menlo Park laboratory he developed the phonograph (1877) and a practical incandescent lamp (1879), and in 1882 he opened the first commercial power station in New York.

personas/marconi/resumen.texto: Italian inventor. He developed wireless telegraphy and in 1901 received a radio signal across the Atlantic; he shared the 1909 Nobel Prize in Physics with Karl Ferdinand Braun.

personas/hermanos-wright/resumen.texto: Wilbur (1867–1912) and Orville Wright (1871–1948), bicycle makers from Dayton, Ohio. On December 17, 1903 they made the first controlled, sustained flight of a powered airplane.

personas/haber/resumen.texto: German chemist. In 1909 he succeeded in synthesizing ammonia from atmospheric nitrogen, the basis of industrial fertilizers (Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1918); in the First World War he directed the German chemical weapons program.

personas/henry-ford/resumen.texto: American businessman, founder of the Ford Motor Company (1903). With the Model T and the moving assembly line (1913) he made the automobile cheaper and spread mass production; in the 1920s he published antisemitic propaganda.

hechos/central-de-pearl-street/resumen.texto: On September 4, 1882, Thomas Edison started up in Lower Manhattan the first commercial power station, which supplied direct current to about 85 customers with 400 lamps.

hechos/transmision-transatlantica-de-mar.texto: On December 12, 1901, Guglielmo Marconi reported having received at Signal Hill (Newfoundland) the letter S in Morse code, sent from Poldhu (Cornwall), about 3,500 km away. Some doubted the reception, but in 1902 he repeated long-distance transmissions.

hechos/primer-vuelo-de-los-wright/titulo.texto: First flight of the Wright brothers

hechos/primer-vuelo-de-los-wright/resume.texto: On December 17, 1903, at Kill Devil Hills, near Kitty Hawk (North Carolina), Orville Wright flew 12 seconds and 37 meters in the Flyer: the first controlled, sustained flight of a powered airplane. They made four flights that day; the longest, of 59 seconds, was piloted by Wilbur.

hechos/proceso-haber-bosch/resumen.texto: In July 1909, at the Karlsruhe Technical University, Fritz Haber showed technicians from the company BASF an apparatus that produced ammonia from atmospheric nitrogen and hydrogen, at high pressure and with a catalyst. Carl Bosch scaled it up to industrial production in 1913; the resulting fertilizers today sustain the food supply of a large part of humanity.

hechos/linea-de-montaje-de-ford/resumen.texto: On December 1, 1913, at the Highland Park plant (Michigan), Ford launched a moving assembly line for the Model T, which cut the time to assemble a car from more than 12 hours to about an hour and a half. The method spread throughout the industry.

hechos/experimento-de-geiger-marsden/res.texto: In Rutherford's laboratory in Manchester, Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden carried out a series of scattering experiments between 1908 and 1913; in 1909 they observed that some alpha particles fired at a thin gold foil bounced back at large angles, a result Rutherford explained in 1911 with the atomic nucleus.

hechos/eclipse-de-1919/resumen.texto: During the total eclipse of May 29, 1919, British expeditions on the island of Príncipe and in Sobral (Brazil) photographed the stars near the Sun. Their deflection matched that predicted by general relativity; the announcement in London, in November, made Einstein famous.

hechos/congreso-solvay-de-1927/resumen.texto: In October 1927, in Brussels, the creators of quantum mechanics discussed how to interpret it; there began the debate between Einstein and Bohr over whether the theory was complete. Seventeen of the 29 attendees had received or would receive the Nobel Prize.

hechos/descubrimiento-de-la-fision/resum.texto: In December 1938, at the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute for Chemistry in Berlin, Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann found barium in uranium bombarded with neutrons; weeks later Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch explained it as the splitting of the nucleus. Laboratories in several countries quickly confirmed that fission released neutrons capable of sustaining a chain reaction.

hechos/chicago-pile-1/titulo.texto: Chicago Pile-1, the first nuclear reactor

hechos/chicago-pile-1/resumen.texto: On December 2, 1942, beneath the stands of a University of Chicago stadium, Enrico Fermi's team achieved the first controlled, self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction, in a pile of graphite and uranium.

hechos/proyecto-manhattan/resumen.texto: US program, with the participation of the United Kingdom and Canada, that developed the first nuclear weapons between 1942 and 1946, building on uranium research the government had funded since 1939. It was led by General Leslie Groves and, at the Los Alamos laboratory, Robert Oppenheimer. It came to employ some 130,000 people at sites such as Oak Ridge, Hanford and Los Alamos.

hechos/prueba-trinity/resumen.texto: On 16 July 1945, in the New Mexico desert, the Manhattan Project detonated the first atomic bomb, a plutonium device, with a yield of 21 kilotons according to the official estimate and 24.8 kilotons according to a new analysis published in 2021. Three weeks later bombs were dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki.

hechos/central-de-obninsk/resumen.texto: In June 1954 the Soviet Obninsk plant, southwest of Moscow, became the first nuclear power plant connected to an electrical grid, with 5 MW of output. It operated until 2002.

hechos/accidente-de-chernobil/resumen.texto: On April 26, 1986, a poorly executed test at reactor 4 of the Chernobyl plant, in Soviet Ukraine, caused an explosion and a fire that spread radioactive material across Europe. A 30 km zone around it was evacuated; it is the worst accident in the history of nuclear power.

hechos/descubrimiento-del-boson-de-higgs.texto: On July 4, 2012, the ATLAS and CMS experiments at CERN's Large Hadron Collider announced the observation of a particle of about 125 GeV consistent with the Higgs boson, predicted in 1964.

hechos/deteccion-de-ondas-gravitacionale.texto: On September 14, 2015, LIGO's two detectors, in Livingston (Louisiana) and Hanford (Washington), recorded seven milliseconds apart the signal of the merger of two black holes. It was announced on February 11, 2016.

hechos/bomba-de-turing/resumen.texto: At Bletchley Park, Alan Turing and Gordon Welchman designed, based on an earlier Polish machine, the electromechanical “bombe” that searched for the daily keys of the German Enigma cipher machine; the first one began operating in 1940.

hechos/colossus/resumen.texto: Electronic vacuum-tube machine designed by Tommy Flowers to decipher high-level German messages encrypted with the Lorenz machine. It operated from early 1944, ten were built, and its existence remained secret until the 1970s.

hechos/eniac/resumen.texto: General-purpose electronic computer built by John Mauchly and J. Presper Eckert for the US Army and unveiled in February 1946. It had about 18,000 vacuum tubes; it was programmed, by rewiring it, by six women mathematicians.

hechos/invencion-del-transistor/resumen.texto: On December 16, 1947, John Bardeen and Walter Brattain got a germanium point-contact amplifier working at Bell Labs, and a week later they demonstrated it to management. The transistor replaced vacuum tubes.

hechos/manchester-baby/resumen.texto: On June 21, 1948, the first program stored in a computer's electronic memory ran at the University of Manchester, on an experimental machine by Frederic Williams, Tom Kilburn and Geoff Tootill.

hechos/conferencia-de-dartmouth/resumen.texto: Gathering of about eight weeks in the summer of 1956 at Dartmouth College, considered the founding event of artificial intelligence as a discipline. Allen Newell and Herbert Simon presented there the Logic Theorist, a program that proved theorems.

hechos/primer-circuito-integrado/resumen.texto: On September 12, 1958, Jack Kilby got an oscillator working at Texas Instruments with all its components on a single piece of germanium. In 1959 Robert Noyce, at Fairchild, designed the silicon version that went into mass production.

hechos/madre-de-todas-las-demos/resumen.texto: On December 9, 1968, at a conference in San Francisco, Douglas Engelbart demonstrated for 90 minutes his laboratory's NLS system: mouse, hypertext, windows, real-time collaborative editing and videoconferencing with colleagues about 50 km away.

hechos/creacion-de-unix/resumen.texto: In the summer of 1969 Ken Thompson wrote at Bell Labs, on an unused PDP-7 minicomputer, the first version of a simple operating system that was later called Unix and that he developed with Dennis Ritchie.

hechos/intel-4004/resumen.texto: In November 1971 Intel released the 4004, a complete 4-bit processor on a single chip, with about 2,300 transistors. It was designed by Federico Faggin, Ted Hoff, Stanley Mazor and Masatoshi Shima for a calculator by the Japanese company Busicom.

hechos/xerox-alto/resumen.texto: Experimental computer from Xerox PARC with a bitmap display, mouse, graphical interface with windows, Ethernet networking and laser printing. It was not sold to the public, but it inspired the Apple Macintosh (1984) and Windows.

hechos/deep-blue-kasparov/resumen.texto: In 1996 world chess champion Garry Kasparov won a first match against IBM's Deep Blue computer; in May 1997, in New York, the machine won 3.5–2.5, the first defeat of a world champion by a computer in a match under tournament time controls. Kasparov alleged irregularities, which IBM denied.

hechos/alexnet-gana-imagenet/resumen.texto: In the 2012 ImageNet image recognition competition, the deep neural network of Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever and Geoffrey Hinton achieved a far lower error than the other entrants (15.3% versus 26.2%), which turned industry and academia toward deep learning.

hechos/alphago-lee-sedol/resumen.texto: In March 2016, in Seoul, DeepMind's AlphaGo program defeated Lee Sedol, one of the world's best go players, 4–1. A machine had not been expected to achieve this for another decade.

hechos/alphafold-casp14/resumen.texto: At CASP14 (2020), the biennial protein structure prediction competition, DeepMind's AlphaFold 2 achieved accuracy comparable to experimental methods for most proteins. In 2021 DeepMind and the European Molecular Biology Laboratory opened a database of predicted structures, which grew to more than 200 million.

hechos/lanzamiento-de-chatgpt/lugar.texto: OpenAI headquarters, Pioneer Building, San Francisco

hechos/lanzamiento-de-chatgpt/resumen.texto: On 30 November 2022 OpenAI opened ChatGPT to the public, a conversational assistant based on a language model fine-tuned with reinforcement learning from human feedback. By some estimates it passed one hundred million users in two months, and it set off a race among generative artificial intelligence companies.

hechos/arpanet/resumen.texto: Computer network funded by ARPA, an agency of the US Department of Defense. The first message was sent on 29 October 1969, from UCLA to the Stanford Research Institute, and by December it connected four nodes. It was the forerunner of the internet and was shut down in 1990.

hechos/adopcion-de-tcp-ip/resumen.texto: On 1 January 1983 the computers on ARPANET switched from the NCP protocol to TCP/IP, which allowed it to be interconnected with other networks. The date is regarded as the birth of the internet, the network of networks.

hechos/nacimiento-de-la-web/titulo.texto: Birth of the World Wide Web

hechos/nacimiento-de-la-web/resumen.texto: Following his 1989 proposal, Tim Berners-Lee launched the first web server and the first browser at CERN in December 1990, on a NeXT computer. On 6 August 1991 he announced the project publicly, and in April 1993 CERN released the software royalty-free.

hechos/mosaic/resumen.texto: Graphical web browser developed at the NCSA of the University of Illinois by Marc Andreessen and Eric Bina, released in 1993. It displayed images alongside text and ran on several operating systems; it took the web beyond academia.

hechos/fundacion-de-google/resumen.texto: Larry Page and Sergey Brin founded Google in September 1998, in a garage in Menlo Park, California, to commercialize the search engine they had developed at Stanford. It became the dominant search engine and one of the largest companies in the world.

hechos/presentacion-del-iphone/resumen.texto: On 9 January 2007, in San Francisco, Steve Jobs unveiled Apple's iPhone, a phone with a multi-touch screen, a full web browser and, from 2008, an app store. It set the model for the smartphone, which within a few years became the main means of accessing the internet.

hechos/descubrimiento-de-la-insulina/res.texto: In 1921, at the University of Toronto, Frederick Banting and Charles Best extracted a substance from dogs' pancreases that lowered blood sugar; in January 1922 it was given for the first time to a patient, Leonard Thompson. The company Eli Lilly began producing it on a large scale in 1923.

hechos/descubrimiento-de-la-penicilina/r.texto: In September 1928, on returning from vacation, Alexander Fleming noticed that a mold had contaminated a culture plate of staphylococci and destroyed the nearby colonies. Penicillin became a medicine only in 1940–1941, through the work of Florey's team at Oxford.

hechos/vacuna-antipolio-de-salk/resumen.texto: On 12 April 1955 the University of Michigan announced that the 1954 field trial, in which 1.8 million children took part, had shown the Salk vaccine to be safe and effective; its use was licensed the same day. Weeks later, improperly inactivated batches from Cutter Laboratories caused cases of polio.

hechos/pildora-anticonceptiva/resumen.texto: In May 1960 the US Food and Drug Administration approved Enovid as an oral contraceptive, developed from the research of Gregory Pincus and John Rock, funded by Margaret Sanger and Katharine McCormick; in 1961 it reached Australia and West Germany. The pill changed family planning and met religious opposition, such as that of the encyclical Humanae vitae (1968).

hechos/desciframiento-del-codigo-genetic.texto: Between 1961 and 1966 the teams of Marshall Nirenberg, Har Gobind Khorana and others established which RNA base triplet corresponds to each of the twenty amino acids in proteins.

hechos/erradicacion-de-la-viruela/resume.texto: On 8 May 1980 the World Health Assembly declared smallpox eradicated, a disease that had killed hundreds of millions of people in the 20th century. It was the result of a worldwide vaccination and surveillance campaign led by the WHO from 1967.

hechos/descubrimiento-del-vih/resumen.texto: In 1983 the team of Luc Montagnier and Françoise Barré-Sinoussi, at the Pasteur Institute in Paris, isolated the retrovirus that causes AIDS, a disease identified in 1981. In 1984 Robert Gallo's team confirmed its role; the priority dispute was settled by an agreement between France and the US in 1987.

hechos/clonacion-de-dolly/resumen.texto: Dolly the sheep was born on 5 July 1996 at the Roslin Institute, near Edinburgh, cloned from a mammary gland cell of an adult sheep; her existence was announced in February 1997. She lived until 2003.

hechos/genoma-humano/resumen.texto: International publicly funded research project, begun in 1990, to determine the complete sequence of the human genome. The draft was announced in June 2000 and published in 2001, and the project was declared complete in April 2003; the gapless sequence was only completed in 2022.

hechos/vacunas-de-arnm-contra-la-covid/r.texto: The vaccine from BioNTech (Mainz) and Pfizer, based on modified messenger RNA, was the first COVID-19 vaccine authorized after a phase 3 trial: the United Kingdom approved it on 2 December 2020, and Moderna's was authorized shortly afterward. They were the first mRNA vaccines in mass use.

hechos/cohete-de-goddard/resumen.texto: On 16 March 1926, on a farm in Auburn, Massachusetts, Robert Goddard launched the first liquid-fueled rocket, powered by gasoline and liquid oxygen, which flew for 2.5 seconds and reached a height of about 12 meters.

hechos/v2-llega-al-espacio/titulo.texto: The V-2, the first object to reach space

hechos/v2-llega-al-espacio/resumen.texto: The German V-2 ballistic missile, developed at Peenemünde under the direction of Wernher von Braun, became in June 1944 the first human-made object to exceed an altitude of 100 km. It was used against London and Antwerp from September 1944, and its production at the underground Mittelwerk factory cost the lives of thousands of prisoners.

hechos/sputnik-1/resumen.texto: On 4 October 1957 the Soviet Union put Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite, into orbit from Baikonur; it was a 58 cm sphere that emitted radio beeps. The launch started the space race and led the US to create NASA in 1958.

hechos/vuelo-de-gagarin/resumen.texto: On 12 April 1961 Soviet cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin made one orbit of the Earth aboard the Vostok 1 spacecraft, in 108 minutes: he was the first human being in space.

hechos/apolo-11/resumen.texto: On 20 July 1969 Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed on the Moon in the lunar module Eagle, while Michael Collins orbited in the command module; the mission had lifted off on 16 July from the Kennedy Space Center and returned on the 24th. An estimated 600 million people followed the broadcast.

hechos/telescopio-hubble/titulo.texto: Launch of the Hubble Space Telescope

hechos/telescopio-hubble/resumen.texto: On 24 April 1990 the space shuttle Discovery put into orbit the Hubble Space Telescope, a project of NASA and the European Space Agency. A flaw in its primary mirror was corrected in 1993 by an astronaut mission; its observations helped pin down the age of the universe and discover its accelerating expansion.

hechos/estacion-espacial-internacional/r.texto: Orbital laboratory built by the space agencies of the US, Russia, Europe, Japan and Canada. Its first module, Zarya, was launched from Baikonur in November 1998, and it has been permanently inhabited since November 2000.

hechos/curva-de-keeling/resumen.texto: In March 1958 Charles David Keeling began measuring atmospheric carbon dioxide at the Mauna Loa Observatory in Hawaii. The series, which continues, shows the rise from about 315 parts per million in 1958 to more than 420 in the 2020s.

hechos/creacion-del-ipcc/resumen.texto: In 1988 the World Meteorological Organization and the United Nations Environment Programme created the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), which periodically assesses climate science. It received the 2007 Nobel Peace Prize, shared with Al Gore.

hechos/bomba-little-boy/resumen.texto: Gun-type atomic bomb designed at Los Alamos by Francis Birch’s group: a charge of cordite fired a hollow cylinder of uranium-235 at a solid one of the same material. It succeeded the Thin Man, a plutonium design abandoned in 1944. It was considered almost certain to work and was never tested before use: the bomb dropped on Hiroshima on 6 August 1945 contained 64 kg of uranium, of which less than 1 kg underwent fission. It exploded with about 15 kilotons (Los Alamos estimate of 1985). According to the Radiation Effects Research Foundation, between 90,000 and 166,000 people died in Hiroshima by the end of 1945, most of them civilians.

hechos/bomba-fat-man/resumen.texto: Implosion-type atomic bomb with a solid plutonium core, made at Los Alamos with plutonium produced at Hanford. When it was confirmed in April 1944 that plutonium from the reactors contained plutonium-240, which would cause a gun-type bomb to detonate prematurely, the laboratory in July reorganized around implosion. The first device, “The Gadget”, exploded in the Trinity test on 16 July 1945 (21 kilotons according to the official estimate and 24.8 according to a new analysis published in 2021), and another fell on Nagasaki on 9 August (21 kilotons). In Nagasaki between 35,000 and 40,000 people died on the spot and between 60,000 and 80,000 in total.

hechos/calutrones-de-oak-ridge/resumen.texto: The calutron, a mass spectrometer that Ernest Lawrence developed from his cyclotron, separates uranium isotopes with electric and magnetic fields. The Y-12 plant at Oak Ridge, whose construction began on 18 February 1943 and whose first building, Alpha, was completed on 1 November 1943, used it on an industrial scale, and its enriched uranium went into the Little Boy bomb. After the war, gaseous diffusion was preferred: more complicated, but more efficient.

hechos/operacion-crossroads/resumen.texto: Two US nuclear tests at Bikini Atoll, Able (1 July 1946) and Baker (25 July, underwater), using Fat Man-type bombs of 23 kilotons against a fleet of 95 ships, to investigate the effects of nuclear weapons on ships. They were the first since Trinity and the first announced in advance and observed by guests and the press; Baker produced the first immediate and concentrated radioactive fallout. The 167 inhabitants of Bikini were relocated, most of them to Rongerik Atoll. The thermonuclear tests of the 1950s left the atoll contaminated, and it remains uninhabited.

hechos/multics/resumen.texto: Time-sharing operating system whose development began in 1964 in Cambridge, Massachusetts, as a project of MIT (Project MAC, with Fernando Corbató), General Electric and Bell Labs, on the GE 645 computer. Bell withdrew in 1969, seeing that it would not yield a useful system in the short term, and part of its team created Unix. Honeywell, which bought GE’s computer division in 1970, developed it until 1985; the last native installation was shut down on 30 October 2000.

hechos/intel-8008/resumen.texto: 8-bit microprocessor that addresses 16 KB, added to Intel’s catalogue in April 1972. Computer Terminal Corporation designed its architecture for the Datapoint 2200 terminal and Intel manufactured it; as CTC did not use it, Intel began selling it to other customers. It was the processor of the first commercial personal computers that were not calculators, not counting the Datapoint 2200 itself (SCELBI, Micral N and MCM/70), and it was followed by the Intel 8080 and the x86 family.

hechos/efecto-mossbauer/resumen.texto: Rudolf Mößbauer, trained at the Technical University of Munich, discovered during his doctoral work at the Max Planck Institute for Medical Research in Heidelberg that the nuclei of a solid can emit and absorb gamma rays without recoil, and published the results with his thesis in 1958. For this he received half of the 1961 Nobel Prize in Physics.

hechos/casete-compacto/resumen.texto: On 28 August 1963, at the Berlin Radio Exhibition, Philips presented the compact cassette, a magnetic-tape format for recording and playing back audio, invented by a team led by Lou Ottens in Hasselt. Philips preferred this two-reel cassette to the single-hole one that its Vienna factory was developing with Grundig, and from 1966 it made the patent available to other manufacturers at no charge.

hechos/gluones-en-desy/titulo.texto: First tests of gluons at DESY

hechos/gluones-en-desy/resumen.texto: In 1978 the PLUTO detector at the DORIS collider at DESY gave the first evidence that certain decays of the Υ(9.46) were interpreted as three-jet events produced by three gluons. In summer 1979, at the PETRA collider, the TASSO, MARK-J and PLUTO experiments clearly observed that three-jet topology, and in 1980 TASSO and PLUTO confirmed that the gluon has spin 1.

hechos/puesta-en-marcha-del-lhc/titulo.texto: Start-up of the Large Hadron Collider

hechos/puesta-en-marcha-del-lhc/resumen.texto: CERN built the LHC between 1998 and 2008 with the collaboration of more than 10,000 scientists. It first ran on 10 September 2008; on 19 September a faulty electrical connection caused a quench of the superconducting magnets that damaged more than 50 of them and halted tests until 20 November 2009. The first collisions were recorded in November 2009, at energies of up to 1.2 TeV per beam; on 30 March 2010 the first collisions at 3.5 TeV per beam took place, and the research programme began.

hechos/descubrimiento-del-neutron/resume.texto: James Chadwick, with the help of Norman Feather, showed at the Cavendish Laboratory that the radiation from beryllium bombarded with alpha particles, previously observed by Bothe and Becker in Giessen and by the Joliot-Curies in Paris, was not gamma rays but uncharged particles with a mass similar to that of the proton. Within a few months Heisenberg and Iwanenko proposed a nucleus of protons and neutrons. 1932 was called the “annus mirabilis” of nuclear physics at the Cavendish.

hechos/descubrimiento-de-la-estructura-d.texto: Discovery of the structure of DNA

On 25 April 1953 Nature published the article by Francis Crick and James Watson with the double-helix model of DNA, supported by X-ray diffraction data collected at King’s College London by Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins. Crick, Watson and Wilkins received the 1962 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. How Watson and Crick gained access to Franklin’s data is a matter of controversy.

hechos/red-npl/titulo.texto: NPL Network, a pioneer of packet switching

hechos/red-npl/resumen.texto: Based on designs that Donald Davies conceived in 1965, the local network of the National Physical Laboratory began development in 1966. Elements of its first version, the Mark I, were working in early 1969, before ARPANET installed its first node, and fully in January 1970; the Mark II operated from 1973 to 1986. It was the first network to implement packet switching and to use high-speed links.

hechos/primer-bebe-por-fecundacion-in-vi.texto: Birth of Louise Brown, the first person born after in vitro fertilization

Louise Brown was born on 25 July 1978 at Oldham General Hospital, by scheduled caesarean section, after a procedure carried out on 10 November 1977 and developed by Patrick Steptoe, Robert Edwards and Jean Purdy. She was called a “test-tube baby”, but conception took place in a Petri dish. Edwards received the 2010 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for this work.

hechos/agujero-de-ozono/titulo.texto: Discovery of the Antarctic ozone hole

hechos/agujero-de-ozono/resumen.texto: Joseph Farman, Brian Gardiner and Jon Shanklin, of the British Antarctic Survey, measured ozone declines from 1982 at Halley station using Dobson spectrophotometers, and in May 1985 published in Nature the first evidence of a seasonal “hole” over Antarctica; later expeditions confirmed that chlorine and bromine from human-made compounds were the cause. In 1987, 43 nations signed the Montreal Protocol, which froze CFC production.

hechos/aislamiento-del-grafeno/resumen.texto: Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov, of the University of Manchester, isolated and characterized sheets of graphene, a single layer of carbon atoms, in 2004 by peeling them from graphite with ordinary adhesive tape (micromechanical exfoliation). Philip Wallace had proposed graphene theoretically in 1947. Geim and Novoselov received the 2010 Nobel Prize in Physics.

hechos/deepmind-aprende-atari/titulo.texto: DeepMind learns to play Atari games

hechos/deepmind-aprende-atari/resumen.texto: DeepMind, founded in London in November 2010 by Demis Hassabis, Shane Legg and Mustafa Suleyman, published in 2013 a reinforcement-learning system using deep Q-learning and convolutional networks that outperformed humans in games such as Pong, Breakout and Enduro. Google confirmed its purchase on 26 January 2014, for a sum reported to have been between 400 and 650 million dollars.

hechos/intel-8080/resumen.texto: 8-bit microprocessor that Intel launched in April 1974 as the successor to the 8008, without being binary-code compatible with it. Federico Faggin was its chief architect, with Masatoshi Shima and Stanley Mazor, and all three are named in its only patent. Its 40-pin package and 16-bit address bus gave access to 64 KB of memory. It was the processor of the first personal computers, such as the Altair 8800, the original processor of the CP/M operating system, and the model on which the assembly language of the x86 family was based.

lugares/bell-labs/resumen.texto: Research laboratory of the telephone company AT&T, headquartered in Murray Hill, New Jersey. The transistor, the silicon solar cell, the Unix operating system and the C language were invented there, and information theory was founded there; its researchers received about ten Nobel Prizes.

lugares/cern/resumen.texto: European Organization for Nuclear Research, on the French-Swiss border near Geneva. It operates the Large Hadron Collider, where the Higgs boson was detected in 2012; in its offices Tim Berners-Lee created the World Wide Web (1989–1991).

lugares/los-alamos/resumen.texto: Secret Manhattan Project laboratory on a mesa in New Mexico, directed by Robert Oppenheimer, where the first atomic bombs were designed. It remains one of the main US nuclear weapons laboratories.

lugares/xerox-parc/resumen.texto: Xerox research center in Palo Alto, California. In the 1970s it developed the Alto computer, the windowed graphical interface, Ethernet, the laser printer and the Smalltalk language, which Apple and Microsoft later brought to market.

lugares/mit/resumen.texto: Research university in Cambridge, Massachusetts. Claude Shannon, Norbert Wiener, John McCarthy and Marvin Minsky worked there; its Radiation Laboratory developed radar in the Second World War, and its artificial intelligence laboratory was one of the first in the world.

lugares/bletchley-park/resumen.texto: Mansion in Buckinghamshire, England, that housed the Government Code and Cypher School during the Second World War. Some 10,000 people, most of them women, broke German Enigma and Lorenz messages there with the help of Turing's “bombes” and Colossus. It is now a museum.

lugares/cabo-canaveral/resumen.texto: Cape on the Atlantic coast of Florida from which the US has launched rockets since 1950. Next to it is the Kennedy Space Center, from which the Apollo missions to the Moon and the space shuttles departed.

lugares/baikonur/resumen.texto: Launch base built by the Soviet Union on the steppe of Kazakhstan, now leased by Russia. Sputnik 1 (1957) and Yuri Gagarin (1961), the first human being in space, departed from there.

lugares/laboratorio-cavendish/resumen.texto: Physics laboratory of the University of Cambridge, first directed by James Clerk Maxwell. The electron (1897) and the neutron (1932) were discovered there, the atom was split for the first time with an accelerator (1932), and Watson and Crick proposed the structure of DNA (1953).

lugares/instituto-de-estudios-avanzados/.texto: Independent research center in Princeton, New Jersey, with no students or classes. Albert Einstein, John von Neumann and Kurt Gödel worked there, and one of the first stored-program computers was built there between 1946 and 1951.

lugares/cold-spring-harbor/resumen.texto: Biology laboratory on Long Island, New York, directed by James Watson from 1968. It was a center of bacterial and viral genetics and of cancer research; from 1910 to 1939 it housed the Eugenics Record Office.

lugares/universidad-de-stanford/resumen.texto: Private university in California, next to Palo Alto. Its industrial park and its graduates gave rise to Silicon Valley; it was one of the first ARPANET nodes, and there Larry Page and Sergey Brin developed the search engine that became Google.

lugares/instituto-pasteur/resumen.texto: Biomedical research foundation created in Paris by Louis Pasteur. The BCG vaccine against tuberculosis was developed there and, in 1983, the AIDS virus (HIV) was isolated there.

lugares/sri-international/resumen.texto: Research institute created by Stanford University in Menlo Park, California, independent since 1970. Douglas Engelbart invented the mouse there, and it was the second ARPANET node (1969).

lugares/instituto-niels-bohr/resumen.texto: Institute of theoretical physics of the University of Copenhagen, founded by Niels Bohr. In the 1920s it brought together Heisenberg, Pauli, Dirac and other creators of quantum mechanics, and gave its name to the “Copenhagen interpretation”.

lugares/universidad-de-gotinga/resumen.texto: University in Lower Saxony, Germany. In the early 20th century it was the leading center of mathematics (Hilbert) and theoretical physics (Born); Heisenberg formulated matrix mechanics there in 1925. The expulsion of Jewish professors in 1933 ended that golden age.

lugares/instituto-roslin/resumen.texto: Animal science research center near Edinburgh, successor to animal genetics bodies created from 1947 onward and now part of the University of Edinburgh. Dolly the sheep, the first mammal cloned from an adult cell, was born there in 1996.

lugares/universidad-de-pensilvania/resum.texto: Private university in Philadelphia. The ENIAC (1946) was built at its Moore School of Electrical Engineering, and there Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman developed the modified messenger RNA used in the COVID-19 vaccines.

lugares/universidad-de-manchester/resume.texto: English university, successor to Owens College (1851). Rutherford discovered the atomic nucleus there (1911), and in 1948 the Manchester Baby, the first stored-program computer, ran there; Alan Turing worked there from 1948.

lugares/hospital-st-mary/resumen.texto: Hospital in the Paddington district of London, with a medical school. In its laboratory Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928.

lugares/observatorio-del-monte-wilson/re.texto: Observatory in the mountains above Pasadena, California. With its Hooker telescope, the largest in the world from 1917 to 1949, Edwin Hubble showed that other galaxies exist and that the universe is expanding.

lugares/universidad-de-toronto/resumen.texto: Public university in Canada. Insulin was isolated there (1921–1922), and Geoffrey Hinton's group developed the deep neural networks that won ImageNet in 2012.
